newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican Indians burn poll stations in Chiapas state.
newsitem.headline: Mexican Indians burn poll stations in Chiapas state.

text.p: Mobs of angry Mexican Indians tore apart dozens of polling stations and blocked roads in the troubled southern state of Chiapas, marring Sunday's national mid-term elections, witnesses said.

The Indians, supporters of the state's Mayan Zapatista rebels, destroyed up to 25 polling stations in the remote central highlands of the impoverished state, they said. Some of the Indians were reportedly masked.
Mexico City's Radio Red said rebel supporters had destroyed a bridge in the area, but the report could not be immediately confirmed.

Witnesses said dozens of Indians stormed polling stations in the villages of San Andres Larrainzar and Tzuben, both about 400 miles (660 km) southeast of Mexico City, tearing down voting booths and setting fire to ballots.
"Get out, get out," they shouted to local election officials in San Andres, who scrambled from the city square.
Polling centres were also reportedly destroyed in the nearby colonial city of San Cristobal de las Casas, the city of Ocosingo, and the towns of Tenejapa and Altamirano.
Other, smaller groups of Indians blocked highways in the area with boulders and tree trunks, witnesses said.

The protests followed a call by Zapatista rebel leader Subcommander Marcos earlier in the week for an election boycott to protest a lack of progress in stalled peace talks between the government and mostly Mayan Indian guerrillas.
Mexicans were voting on Sunday for most of a new Congress, six state governors and a first-ever Mexico City mayor.
The Zapatistas launched an uprising for Indian rights and democracy on New Year's Day 1994, but have since been mired in on-and-off peace talks with the government.
The Zapatistas also accuse local officials of turning a blind eye to violence between wealthy landowners and Indians trying to take over their land.

After Marcos called the boycott, federal election officials decided not to install 23 polling stations in so-called Zapatista territory, a swath of land in the state controlled by rebels and believed to be home to about 40,000 Indians.
Zapatista supporters had vowed late on Saturday to block voting booths in certain parts of the state, even outside Zapatista-controlled territory.
The Zapatistas, disillusioned with local authorities, do not recognise most of Chiapas's elected officials and have set up parallel governments, with "rebel" mayors and city councillors.
